newsitem.title: UK: Northern Ireland economy needs confidence boost.
newsitem.headline: Northern Ireland economy needs confidence boost.

text.p: Northern Ireland's economy should accelerate in 1997 as it benefits from a pick-up in its main export markets but a lack of confidence could threaten progress, a survey by accountants Coopers & Lybrand showed on Thursday.

"Despite slower growth in 1996, the Northern Ireland economy remains in good health in almost every major area," Coopers & Lybrand said. "All the indicators suggest that things should improve significantly during 1997."

The survey found that the economy grew at two percent last year. The upsurge in growth and output experienced in 1995 flattened but much of this was due to sluggishness in Northern Ireland's main export markets, the survey said.

The province's economy is expected to grow at a rate of 2.5 percent in 1997, slightly behind the projected British average of 3.25 percent but with the potential to overtake Britain again in 1998, the survey says.
But Coopers & Lybrand said the extent to which the region's economy would really accelerate may have as much to do with confidence as with opportunity.

A majority of indigenous Northern Irish companies surveyed lacked confidence about the future of the local economy despite increased profits, greater exports, anticipated growing order books and positive investment plans.

"Almost all their lack of confidence appears to reflect unfavourable media coverage of Northern Ireland. Companies believed that bad international publicity could create doubts in export markets over reliability of supply," the survey said.

In addition to concerns about the security situation in the province following the breakdown of the Irish Republican Army's ceasefire and last summer's disturbances, Coopers & Lybrand said there were worries about public spending cuts in 1997.

Total expenditure for the province has been cut by 1.5 percent in real terms for 1997/98 and could have serious implications for both jobs and publicly-funded programmes in Northern Ireland, the survey said.

"There is every chance of a continuing net loss of up to 2,000 civil service jobs inside three years. There is no question that wholesale cuts in government spending could destabilise the province's economy," Coopers & Lybrand said.
The firm also found that the BSE crisis in the beef industry was the greatest crisis ever to hit Northern Irish agriculture.

Almost 80 percent of agribusiness chief executives surveyed believed that BSE represented a long-term problem for the industry while 70 percent expected the crisis to continue to affect their business in 1997.

Coopers & Lybrand said the Northern Irish economy was in good shape and could deliver further growth, properity and international competitiveness but creating a climate of confidence must be a priority of government and politicians.
"It is essential that the business community and indigenous firms in particular have the confidence to invest," it said.
